goals: Explain the uses of genetically modified crops
Explain how Bt toxin protects cotton from insect pests
Explain how RNA interference protects tobacco from a nematode

slides.heading: Biotechnology and its Applications
slides.body_md: Part 1 — how genetically modified crops can reduce losses and the use of chemical pesticides.

visual.alt: Flow showing three options for raising food production

slides.narration: To grow more food, farmers can use more fertilisers and pesticides, farm organically, or use crops that are genetically engineered. Plants, bacteria, fungi and animals whose genes have been altered by manipulation are called genetically modified organisms, or GMOs. In this part we see how GM crops can help.

slides.heading: Why genetically modified crops?
slides.body_md: GM plants have been useful in many ways.

rows: Prevents early exhaustion of soil fertility
Golden rice, rich in vitamin A
Tailor-made plants supplying starches, fuels and pharmaceuticals

visual.alt: Table of benefits of genetically modified crops with examples

slides.narration: GM crops can be made to resist drought or salt, to fight off pests so less pesticide is sprayed, to keep longer after harvest, and to use soil minerals more efficiently. Golden rice was engineered to be rich in vitamin A. Tailor-made plants can also supply raw materials for industries.

slides.heading: Bt: a bacterial insecticide
slides.body_md: ***Bacillus thuringiensis*** (Bt) forms protein crystals containing an **insecticidal protein**. Bt toxins kill certain insects — **lepidopterans** (tobacco budworm, armyworm), **coleopterans** (beetles) and **dipterans** (flies, mosquitoes).

visual.alt: Table of cry genes and the pests they control

slides.narration: The toxin genes, called cry genes, are taken from the bacterium and put into crop plants such as cotton. The plant now makes the insecticidal protein itself, so a caterpillar that feeds on it is killed. Different cry genes control different pests, which lets scientists choose the right gene for each crop.

slides.heading: How Bt toxin kills
slides.body_md: The toxin exists as an **inactive protoxin**, so the bacterium is not harmed. In the insect gut, the **alkaline pH** solubilises the crystals and activates the toxin, which binds to **midgut epithelial cells**, makes **pores**, and causes the cells to **swell and lyse**.

slides.narration: Why does the toxin not kill the bacterium that makes it? Because it is made in an inactive form. Only inside the alkaline gut of an insect is it switched on. The active toxin punches holes in the cells lining the gut, which swell and burst, and the insect dies. The human stomach is acidic, so this activation does not occur there.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: is Bt cotton worth it?
slides.body_md: A farmer’s cotton yield rose from 1.6 to 2.1 tonnes per hectare after switching to Bt cotton, while insecticide sprays fell from 9 to 3 per season. Calculate both changes.
bullets: Yield rise $= \dfrac{2.1 - 1.6}{1.6} \times 100 \approx 31.3$ percent.
Spray reduction $= \dfrac{9 - 3}{9} \times 100 \approx 66.7$ percent.
Interpretation — the plant protects itself from bollworms, so less insecticide is needed; other pests may still need control.

visual.alt: Worked table: yield up 31.3 percent and sprays down 66.7 percent

slides.narration: The yield rose by about thirty-one percent and spraying fell by about sixty-seven percent. Fewer sprays save money and reduce harm to useful insects and to the farmer’s health. Bt protects only against certain insects, though, so farmers still need to watch for other pests.

slides.heading: Pest-resistant plants: the nematode problem
slides.body_md: A nematode, ***Meloidogyne incognita***, infects the roots of tobacco plants and causes a great reduction in yield. A novel strategy based on **RNA interference (RNAi)** prevents this infestation.

rows: In all eukaryotic organisms, as a method of cellular defence
Silences a specific mRNA because a complementary double-stranded RNA binds to it and prevents translation
Infection by RNA viruses, or mobile genetic elements (transposons) that replicate via an RNA intermediate

visual.alt: Table of features of RNA interference

slides.narration: RNA interference is a natural defence. When a double-stranded RNA matching a particular messenger RNA appears in a cell, it binds to that messenger and stops it from being translated. Scientists use this to switch off a chosen gene, here a gene the nematode needs to survive.

slides.heading: RNAi protects tobacco
slides.body_md: Using ***Agrobacterium*** vectors, **nematode-specific genes** were introduced into tobacco so that the plant produces **both sense and antisense RNA**. These form **dsRNA**, which starts RNAi and **silences** the specific mRNA of the nematode.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: Bt or RNAi?
slides.body_md: Match each problem to a biotechnological solution and explain briefly.
bullets: Bollworm caterpillars eating cotton bolls → **Bt cotton** with cryIAc/cryIIAb: toxin activated in the insect’s alkaline gut.
Corn borer damaging maize → **Bt maize** with cryIAb.
Nematodes infecting tobacco roots → **RNAi**: plant makes dsRNA that silences a nematode mRNA.
Children short of vitamin A in a rice-eating region → **golden rice**, rich in vitamin A.

visual.alt: Worked table matching four problems to GM solutions

slides.narration: Pick the solution by asking what the target is. Insects that chew leaves or bolls are killed by Bt toxins, and the right cry gene is chosen for each pest. Nematodes, which are worms, are tackled by silencing one of their genes with RNA interference. And nutritional problems can be addressed by crops with enhanced nutrients.

slides.heading: Summary
bullets: GMOs: tolerance to abiotic stress, pest resistance, fewer post-harvest losses, better mineral use, enhanced nutrition (golden rice).
Bt (Bacillus thuringiensis) toxin: inactive protoxin; activated by alkaline insect gut; binds midgut cells, forms pores, lysis.
cry genes: cryIAc and cryIIAb (cotton bollworms), cryIAb (corn borer).
RNAi: dsRNA silences a specific mRNA; nematode Meloidogyne incognita controlled in tobacco using sense and antisense RNA via Agrobacterium vectors.

visual.alt: Summary table of two pest-resistance techniques

slides.narration: To recap: GM crops can raise yields and reduce pesticide use. Bt crops make an insect-killing toxin that is activated only in insect guts. RNA interference lets plants silence essential genes of pests such as nematodes.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: Explain **why** the toxin does not harm the bacterium (protoxin) and **where** it is activated (alkaline gut).
Name **cry genes** with the pests they control.
Write the RNAi sequence: **genes in → sense + antisense RNA → dsRNA → mRNA silenced**.
slides.narration: Exam tips. Explain the protoxin and its activation in the alkaline gut. Learn the cry genes with their pests. And write the RNA interference steps in order.

slides.heading: Biotechnology in medicine
slides.body_md: Part 2 — safer medicines, gene therapy and early diagnosis.

visual.alt: Flow of applications of biotechnology in medicine

slides.narration: Recombinant DNA technology has changed health care. It enables mass production of safe and more effective medicines, which do not cause unwanted immune reactions as products from non-human sources may. About thirty recombinant therapeutics have been approved worldwide, and twelve of these are marketed in India.

slides.heading: Insulin: two chains
slides.body_md: Insulin is made of **two short polypeptide chains**, **A** (21 amino acids) and **B** (30 amino acids), linked by **disulphide bridges**. In the body it is synthesised as **proinsulin**, which has an extra **C peptide** that is removed during maturation.

visual.alt: Proinsulin with its C peptide and mature insulin with chains A and B joined by disulphide bridges

slides.narration: Insulin controls blood sugar and is needed by people with diabetes. Its structure is the challenge. The body makes it as one longer chain, proinsulin, and then cuts out a middle piece, the C peptide, leaving two chains joined by disulphide bridges. Bacteria cannot carry out this processing.

slides.heading: Making human insulin in bacteria
slides.body_md: Insulin from slaughtered cattle and pigs caused **allergic or other reactions** in some patients. In **1983**, **Eli Lilly**, an American company, prepared two DNA sequences for the **A and B chains**, introduced them into **plasmids of E. coli**, produced the chains **separately**, extracted them and **joined them by creating disulphide bonds**, forming human insulin (Humulin).

nodes.label: DNA for chain A and DNA for chain B
Each inserted into an E. coli plasmid
Chains A and B made separately

visual.alt: Flow of recombinant production of human insulin

slides.narration: Because bacteria cannot remove a C peptide, the trick was to make the two final chains separately. Each chain’s DNA was put into bacteria, the chains were collected and then joined chemically with disulphide bonds. The result is identical to human insulin and avoids the reactions caused by animal insulin.

slides.heading: Quick check: insulin
slides.body_md: Why were chains A and B made separately in E. coli?
slides.narration: Quick check. Can bacteria remove the C peptide from proinsulin?

slides.heading: Worked example 1: counting insulin
slides.body_md: (a) How many amino acids are there in one molecule of mature insulin? (b) Why is the C peptide not counted?
bullets: (a) Chain A $+$ chain B $= 21 + 30 = 51$ amino acids.
(b) The C peptide is part of proinsulin but is **removed** during maturation, so it is not part of mature insulin.
So recombinant production makes only the two final chains, which together contain all the amino acids of mature insulin.

visual.alt: Worked table: 21 plus 30 equals 51 amino acids

slides.narration: Add the two chains: twenty-one plus thirty gives fifty-one amino acids. The C peptide is cut away when proinsulin matures, so it is not counted. This is exactly why the manufacturers produced only chains A and B.

slides.heading: Gene therapy
slides.body_md: **Gene therapy** corrects a gene defect diagnosed in a child or embryo by **inserting a normal gene** into the person’s cells to take over the function of the non-functional gene. The first clinical gene therapy was given in **1990** to a 4-year-old girl with **adenosine deaminase (ADA) deficiency**.

rows: Cells are not immortal: periodic infusions needed
Gene introduced into early embryonic cells (bone-marrow stem cells)

visual.alt: Table of treatments for ADA deficiency and their limitations

slides.narration: ADA is an enzyme crucial for the immune system to work. Its deficiency, caused by deletion of the gene, leaves the child unable to fight infections. Bone marrow transplants and enzyme injections help but do not fully cure. Gene therapy gives the child’s own cells a working copy of the gene.

slides.heading: How ADA gene therapy is done
slides.body_md: **Lymphocytes** are taken from the patient’s blood and grown in culture. A functional **ADA cDNA** is introduced into them using a **retroviral vector**, and the cells are returned to the patient.

nodes.label: Functional ADA cDNA added with a retroviral vector

visual.alt: Flow of gene therapy for ADA deficiency

slides.narration: A disarmed retrovirus carries a working copy of the ADA gene into the lymphocytes. The corrected cells make ADA and help the immune system. Because these cells eventually die, the treatment must be repeated. A permanent cure may be possible if the gene is introduced into bone-marrow cells at an early embryonic stage.

slides.heading: Quick check: gene therapy
slides.body_md: Why does gene therapy using a patient’s lymphocytes need to be repeated periodically?
slides.narration: Quick check. Do mature lymphocytes live for ever?

slides.heading: Molecular diagnosis
slides.body_md: Early diagnosis is essential for effective treatment, but conventional methods (serum and urine analysis) cannot detect infection early. **PCR**, **recombinant DNA technology** and **ELISA** allow early diagnosis.

rows: Amplifies very small amounts of a pathogen’s DNA or RNA: detects HIV in suspected AIDS patients; detects mutations in suspected cancer patients and genetic disorders

A single-stranded DNA or RNA tagged with a radioactive molecule hybridises to its complementary DNA in a clone of cells; detected by autoradiography (a clone with a mutated gene does not appear on the film)
Based on antigen–antibody interaction: detects antigens of the pathogen or antibodies made against it

visual.alt: Table of molecular diagnostic techniques and how each helps

slides.narration: By the time a pathogen is numerous enough to cause symptoms, the disease may be advanced. PCR can detect even a few copies of a pathogen’s genes, so infections like HIV can be found very early. Probes find specific genes, and ELISA detects the antigen or antibodies to it.

slides.heading: Stem cell technology
slides.body_md: **Stem cells** are unspecialised cells that can divide and give rise to many kinds of specialised cells. Stem cell technology aims to use them to **replace damaged cells or tissues** and to study disease.

rows: Stem cells can form many cell types
Cells of the inner cell mass of the early embryo
Give rise to blood cells; used in bone marrow transplants
Repair or replace damaged tissues; gene therapy in early embryonic cells for a permanent cure

visual.alt: Table of the main ideas of stem cell technology

slides.narration: Stem cells are like blank cells that can become many different kinds. Bone-marrow stem cells, for example, make all our blood cells, which is why bone marrow transplants work. Scientists hope to use stem cells to repair damaged tissues, and introducing a corrected gene into such cells could give a lasting cure.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: choosing a diagnostic test
slides.body_md: Suggest a suitable method for each situation and give a reason.
bullets: A person exposed to HIV a short time ago, before antibodies are plentiful → **PCR** to detect viral genetic material at very low levels.
Checking whether a cloned gene carries a known mutation → **labelled DNA probe** and autoradiography.
Screening many blood samples for antibodies to a pathogen → **ELISA**.

rows: Amplifies tiny amounts of nucleic acid

visual.alt: Worked table matching three diagnostic situations to methods

slides.narration: Match the method to what is being detected. Nucleic acid in tiny amounts calls for PCR. A specific sequence or mutation calls for a labelled probe. Antigens or antibodies call for ELISA, which is also convenient for testing many samples.

slides.heading: Quick check: ELISA
slides.body_md: Judge the assertion and the reason about ELISA.
slides.narration: Quick check. What interaction is ELISA based on?

slides.heading: Summary
bullets: About 30 recombinant therapeutics approved worldwide; 12 marketed in India.
Insulin: chains A (21) and B (30) with disulphide bridges; proinsulin has a C peptide. Eli Lilly (1983): chains made separately in E. coli and joined.
Gene therapy: first in 1990 for ADA deficiency; lymphocytes + ADA cDNA via retroviral vector; periodic infusions; permanent cure if gene is put into early embryonic cells.
Molecular diagnosis: PCR (HIV, cancer mutations), radioactive probes with autoradiography, ELISA (antigen–antibody).
Stem cells: unspecialised cells that can form many cell types; potential to repair tissues.

visual.alt: Summary table of medical applications

slides.narration: To recap: recombinant insulin is made by producing chains A and B separately in bacteria. Gene therapy gives patients a working copy of a defective gene, first done for ADA deficiency. PCR, probes and ELISA allow early, precise diagnosis, and stem cells offer hope for repairing tissues.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: Explain why **chains A and B** are made separately (C peptide).
Describe **ADA gene therapy** step by step and why it is **not permanent**.
Give **two uses of PCR** in diagnosis.
State the **basis of ELISA**.
slides.narration: Exam tips. Explain the C peptide problem in insulin production. Describe ADA gene therapy and why it must be repeated. Give two diagnostic uses of PCR. And state that ELISA works through antigen and antibody interaction.

goals: State the uses of transgenic animals with examples

slides.heading: Transgenic animals and ethical issues
slides.body_md: Part 3 — animals with foreign genes, and the rules and rights that should govern biotechnology.

visual.alt: Flow from transgenic animals and their uses to ethical questions and regulation

slides.narration: Animals whose DNA has been manipulated to possess and express an extra, foreign gene are called transgenic animals. Rats, rabbits, pigs, sheep, cows and fish have been made transgenic, but over ninety-five percent of all existing transgenic animals are mice. Their uses raise important ethical questions.

slides.heading: Uses of transgenic animals
slides.body_md: Transgenic animals are made to study biology and to produce useful substances.

rows: Study of genes for growth factors such as insulin-like growth factor
Models for cancer, cystic fibrosis, rheumatoid arthritis and Alzheimer’s disease
α-1-antitrypsin to treat emphysema; products for phenylketonuria and cystic fibrosis
Transgenic mice to test the safety of polio vaccine
Animals with genes that make them more sensitive to toxic substances

visual.alt: Table of uses of transgenic animals with examples

slides.narration: Transgenic animals help us understand how genes control growth and how diseases develop, so that new treatments can be tested. They can also act as living factories, producing valuable human proteins in their milk. And they can make safety testing of vaccines and chemicals faster and more reliable.

slides.heading: Rosie, the transgenic cow
slides.body_md: In **1997**, the first transgenic cow, **Rosie**, produced **human protein-enriched milk** (**2.4 grams per litre**). The milk contained the human **alpha-lactalbumin** and was nutritionally a **more balanced product for human babies** than natural cow’s milk.

rows: Nutritionally more balanced for human babies

visual.alt: Table of facts about Rosie the transgenic cow

slides.narration: Rosie carried a human gene and produced milk containing a human protein. This shows how animals can be used to make proteins that would be hard or costly to make otherwise, by simply collecting their milk.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: how much protein?
slides.body_md: Rosie’s milk contained 2.4 g of human alpha-lactalbumin per litre. How much of the protein is present in 5 litres?
bullets: Protein $= 2.4\ \text{g/L} \times 5\ \text{L} = 12\ \text{g}$.
Idea — collecting milk is a simple, non-invasive way to harvest a recombinant protein.

visual.alt: Worked table: 5 litres contain 12 grams

slides.narration: Multiply the concentration by the volume: two point four grams per litre times five litres gives twelve grams. Animals that secrete a protein in their milk can supply it continuously, which is one reason transgenic animals are attractive for producing human proteins.

slides.heading: Quick check: transgenic animals
slides.body_md: Which animals make up more than 95 percent of all existing transgenic animals?
slides.narration: Quick check. Think of the most common laboratory animal.

slides.heading: Biosafety and GEAC
slides.body_md: Genetic modification may have **unpredictable results** when such organisms are introduced into an ecosystem. The Indian Government set up the **Genetic Engineering Approval Committee (GEAC)**.

rows: The safety of introducing GM organisms for public services

visual.alt: Table of the decisions made by GEAC and why

slides.narration: Manipulating organisms raises ethical concerns. We cannot always predict how a GM organism will behave in the wild or affect other species. So GEAC examines whether GM research is valid and whether releasing a GM organism for public use is safe.

slides.heading: Patents and biopiracy
slides.body_md: Companies may seek **patents** on biological resources and on products derived from them. **Biopiracy** is the use of bio-resources by multinational companies and other organisations **without proper authorisation** from the countries and people concerned, **without compensatory payment**.

rows: India has at least 27 documented varieties. In 1997 an American company got patent rights on basmati rice through the US Patent and Trademark Office, for a new variety derived from Indian farmers’ varieties crossed with semi-dwarf varieties
Attempts were made to patent uses, products and processes based on traditional Indian knowledge
The Indian Parliament cleared the second amendment of the Indian Patents Bill to address patent terms, emergency provisions and research and development initiatives

visual.alt: Table of patent and biopiracy cases involving India

slides.narration: Industrialised nations are rich financially but poor in biodiversity and traditional knowledge, while developing nations like India are rich in both. When companies patent products based on traditional knowledge or local varieties without permission or sharing benefits, it is biopiracy. India now protects its bio-resources and traditional knowledge through law.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: is it biopiracy?
slides.body_md: Decide whether each case is biopiracy and give a reason.
bullets: A foreign company patents a cream based on a traditional Indian medicinal plant use, without asking or paying the communities → **biopiracy**: unauthorised use without compensation.
An Indian university develops a new rice variety with farmers, shares benefits and registers it legally → **not biopiracy**: authorised, with benefit sharing.

A company crosses traditional basmati varieties with semi-dwarf rice and patents the result abroad without India’s consent → **biopiracy concern**: derived from Indian varieties without authorisation.

visual.alt: Worked table judging three cases for biopiracy

slides.narration: Check two things: was there proper authorisation from the country and people concerned, and were the benefits shared? If both are missing, it is biopiracy. Legal registration with consent and benefit sharing is not.

slides.body_md: Judge the assertion and the reason about biopiracy.

slides.heading: Quick check: GEAC
slides.body_md: What is the role of GEAC in India?
slides.narration: Quick check. Recall the two kinds of decisions it makes.

slides.heading: Summary
bullets: Transgenic animals (over 95 percent mice): physiology, disease models, biological products (α-1-antitrypsin), vaccine safety (polio vaccine in mice), chemical safety.
Rosie (1997): human alpha-lactalbumin in milk, 2.4 g per litre.
GEAC: validity of GM research and safety of releasing GM organisms.
Biopiracy: use of bio-resources without authorisation or compensation; basmati (1997), turmeric, neem; second amendment of the Indian Patents Bill.

rows: Carries and expresses a foreign gene

visual.alt: Summary table of key terms

slides.narration: To recap: transgenic animals help research and produce valuable proteins, like Rosie’s milk. Because GM organisms can have unpredictable effects, GEAC regulates research and release in India. And biopiracy, using bio-resources and traditional knowledge without permission or payment, is opposed through patent laws.

sections.heading: 1. Biotechnological applications in agriculture
sections.body_md:
Three options for increasing food production: **agrochemical-based agriculture**, **organic agriculture** and **genetically engineered crop-based agriculture**. Plants, bacteria, fungi and animals whose genes have been altered by manipulation are **genetically modified organisms (GMOs)**.

**Uses of GM plants:** tolerance to abiotic stresses (cold, drought, salt, heat); reduced reliance on chemical pesticides (pest-resistant crops); reduced post-harvest losses; increased efficiency of mineral use (prevents early exhaustion of soil fertility); enhanced nutritional value (**golden rice**, rich in vitamin A); tailor-made plants supplying alternative resources to industries (starches, fuels, pharmaceuticals).

**Bt crops.** *Bacillus thuringiensis* forms protein crystals with an insecticidal protein. The Bt toxin kills **lepidopterans** (tobacco budworm, armyworm), **coleopterans** (beetles) and **dipterans** (flies, mosquitoes).
- The toxin is an **inactive protoxin**, so the bacterium is not killed.
- In the insect gut the **alkaline pH** solubilises the crystals and activates the toxin.
- The active toxin binds to the surface of **midgut epithelial cells** and creates **pores**, causing **swelling and lysis**; the insect dies.
- The toxin is coded by **cry genes**: **cryIAc** and **cryIIAb** control **cotton bollworms**; **cryIAb** controls **corn borer**.

**Pest-resistant plants by RNA interference (RNAi).** The nematode ***Meloidogyne incognita*** infects tobacco roots and reduces yield. RNAi occurs in all eukaryotes as a method of cellular defence: it silences a specific mRNA because a complementary **double-stranded RNA (dsRNA)** binds to it and prevents translation. Natural sources of dsRNA are infection by RNA viruses and mobile genetic elements (transposons) that replicate via an RNA intermediate.
- Using ***Agrobacterium*** vectors, **nematode-specific genes** were introduced into the host plant.
- The plant produced **both sense and antisense RNA**, which formed dsRNA and started RNAi.
- The specific mRNA of the nematode was silenced, so the parasite **could not survive** in the transgenic host.

sections.heading: 2. Biotechnological applications in medicine
sections.body_md:
Recombinant DNA technology allows mass production of **safe and more effective** therapeutic drugs that do not cause unwanted immunological responses, as similar products from non-human sources can. About **30 recombinant therapeutics** have been approved for human use worldwide; **12** are marketed in India.

**Genetically engineered insulin.** Insulin from the pancreas of slaughtered cattle and pigs caused allergy or other reactions in some patients.
- Mature insulin has **two short polypeptide chains, A and B**, linked by **disulphide bridges** (chain A 21 and chain B 30 amino acids, 51 in all).
- In mammals it is made as a **prohormone (proinsulin)** with an extra stretch, the **C peptide**, which is removed during maturation. Bacteria cannot carry out this step.
- In **1983**, **Eli Lilly** prepared two DNA sequences for chains A and B, introduced them into **plasmids of E. coli**, produced the chains separately, extracted them and combined them by creating disulphide bonds to form human insulin.

**Gene therapy** corrects a gene defect diagnosed in a child or embryo: genes are inserted into the person’s cells and tissues, and a normal gene compensates for the non-functional one.
- First clinical use: **1990**, a **4-year-old girl** with **adenosine deaminase (ADA) deficiency**. ADA is crucial for the immune system; the disorder results from **deletion of the ADA gene**.
- Other treatments: bone marrow transplantation; enzyme replacement therapy (functional ADA by injection) — neither is completely curative.
- Method: **lymphocytes** from the patient’s blood are grown in culture; a functional **ADA cDNA** is introduced using a **retroviral vector**; the cells are returned to the patient. Lymphocytes are **not immortal**, so periodic infusions are needed.
- If the gene isolated from marrow cells producing ADA is introduced into cells at **early embryonic stages**, it **could be a permanent cure**.

**Molecular diagnosis.** Conventional methods (serum and urine analysis) cannot detect a disease early.
- **PCR** amplifies very low concentrations of a pathogen’s nucleic acid: used to detect **HIV** in suspected AIDS patients and **mutations** in suspected cancer patients; also used to identify many other genetic disorders.
- A single-stranded DNA or RNA tagged with a **radioactive molecule (probe)** hybridises to its complementary DNA in a clone of cells and is detected by **autoradiography**; a clone with a mutated gene does not appear on the photographic film because the probe is not complementary to it.
- **ELISA** works on the principle of **antigen–antibody interaction**: it detects antigens of the pathogen, or antibodies made against it.

**Stem cell technology.** Stem cells are unspecialised cells that can divide and form many kinds of specialised cells (for example, bone-marrow stem cells form blood cells). They hold promise for repairing or replacing damaged tissues and, with gene therapy in early embryonic cells, for lasting cures.

Correction of a gene defect by inserting a normal gene into a person’s cells.
An immune disorder caused by deletion of the gene for adenosine deaminase.
Enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay: a test based on antigen–antibody interaction.

sections.heading: 3. Transgenic animals
sections.body_md:
Animals whose DNA has been manipulated to possess and express an extra (foreign) gene are **transgenic animals**. Transgenic rats, rabbits, pigs, sheep, cows and fish have been produced, but **over 95 percent** of all existing transgenic animals are **mice**.

**Uses:**
- **Normal physiology and development** — study of how genes are regulated and how their products affect body functions and development, e.g. insulin-like growth factor.
- **Study of disease** — models for human diseases such as **cancer, cystic fibrosis, rheumatoid arthritis and Alzheimer’s disease**, so that new treatments can be investigated.
- **Biological products** — medicines made from biological products can be expensive; transgenic animals that produce useful products can be made, e.g. human protein **α-1-antitrypsin** used to treat **emphysema**; attempts for products to treat phenylketonuria and cystic fibrosis.
- **Vaccine safety** — transgenic mice are used to test the safety of the **polio vaccine** before it is used on humans.
- **Chemical safety (toxicity) testing** — animals carrying genes that make them more sensitive to toxic substances give results in less time.

**Rosie (1997):** the first transgenic cow; produced human protein-enriched milk (**2.4 grams per litre**) containing human **alpha-lactalbumin**, nutritionally more balanced for human babies than natural cow milk.

sections.heading: 4. Ethical issues
sections.body_md:
Manipulation of living organisms needs regulation, because genetic modification may have **unpredictable results** when such organisms enter an ecosystem.

**GEAC.** The Indian Government set up the **Genetic Engineering Approval Committee**, which makes decisions on the **validity of GM research** and the **safety of introducing GM organisms** for public services.

**Patents and biopiracy.**
- There is growing public anger that certain companies are granted **patents** for products and technologies that use genetic materials, plants and other biological resources long identified, developed and used by farmers and indigenous people.
- **Basmati rice:** India has an estimated **200 000** varieties of rice, including at least **27** documented varieties of basmati. In **1997** an American company got patent rights on basmati rice through the US Patent and Trademark Office, for a new variety derived from Indian farmers’ varieties crossed with semi-dwarf varieties; it was claimed as an invention.
- Other traditional Indian products, such as **turmeric** and **neem**, have also been subjects of patent attempts.
- **Biopiracy:** the use of bio-resources by multinational companies and other organisations **without proper authorisation** from the countries and people concerned, **without compensatory payment**.
- Industrialised nations are rich financially but poor in biodiversity and traditional knowledge; developing and under-developed nations are rich in both. Some nations are developing laws to prevent unauthorised exploitation of bio-resources and traditional knowledge.
- The Indian Parliament has cleared the **second amendment of the Indian Patents Bill**, which takes such issues into consideration, including patent terms, emergency provisions, and research and development initiatives.

A right granted by a government to an inventor to prevent others from commercially using the invention.
Use of bio-resources without proper authorisation from the countries and people concerned and without compensatory payment.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Common mistakes**
- Saying Bt toxin is active inside the bacterium (it is an inactive protoxin).
- Saying the toxin is activated by acidic pH (the insect gut is alkaline).
- Mixing up the cry genes for cotton bollworm and corn borer.
- Saying insulin was made in E. coli as proinsulin (chains A and B were made separately).
- Forgetting why gene therapy with lymphocytes must be repeated (lymphocytes are not immortal).
- Defining biopiracy without both conditions: no authorisation and no compensation.

**How marks are usually awarded**
- 1-mark items: organism, gene, year, enzyme, committee.
- 2–3-mark answers: mechanism of Bt toxin; RNAi steps; insulin production; uses of transgenic animals.
- 5-mark answers: Bt cotton and RNAi together; gene therapy for ADA deficiency with molecular diagnosis; ethical issues with Indian examples.
- Case-based items: field data on Bt crops, insulin production, diagnosis choices or a biopiracy scenario, with a 2-mark part with an internal choice.

questions.stem_md: Explain why Bt toxin harms a bollworm feeding on Bt cotton but does not harm the bacterium that produces it.

answer.model_answer_md: The bacterium makes the toxin as an **inactive protoxin** in crystals, so it is not harmed. In the bollworm’s gut the **alkaline pH** dissolves the crystals and **activates** the toxin, which binds to **midgut epithelial cells**, creates **pores**, and makes them swell and burst, killing the insect.

questions.solution_md: Protoxin; activation by alkaline gut and lysis of midgut cells.

marking_scheme.step: Alkaline activation, pores and lysis in the insect

questions.stem_md: Describe how RNA interference was used to make tobacco plants resistant to the nematode Meloidogyne incognita.

answer.model_answer_md: Using **Agrobacterium** vectors, **nematode-specific genes** were introduced into tobacco. The transgenic plant produced **both sense and antisense RNA** from these genes. Being complementary, they paired to form **double-stranded RNA (dsRNA)**, which started **RNA interference**. When the nematode fed on the roots, the dsRNA **silenced** its matching **mRNA**, so an essential protein was not made and the parasite **could not survive** in the transgenic host.

questions.solution_md: Gene transfer, dsRNA formation, silencing of nematode mRNA.

marking_scheme.step: Sense and antisense RNA form dsRNA

questions.stem_md: A farming district faces three problems: frequent drought, heavy losses of grain in storage, and children short of vitamin A. Suggest how genetically modified crops could help with each problem.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Drought:** GM crops made **tolerant to abiotic stresses** such as drought could grow with less water.

2. **Storage losses:** GM crops engineered to **reduce post-harvest losses** would spoil more slowly.

3. **Vitamin A:** crops with **enhanced nutritional value**, such as **golden rice** rich in vitamin A, could improve children’s diets.

questions.solution_md: Match each problem to a GM trait.

questions.stem_md: Explain how biotechnology has produced pest-resistant crops, using Bt cotton and RNAi tobacco as examples.

answer.model_answer_md:
**Bt cotton.** The soil bacterium Bacillus thuringiensis makes crystal proteins that kill certain insects. The toxin is coded by cry genes; cryIAc and cryIIAb control cotton bollworms and cryIAb controls corn borer. These genes were introduced into cotton, so the plant makes the toxin itself. The toxin is an inactive protoxin; when a bollworm eats the plant, the alkaline pH of its gut solubilises the crystals and activates the toxin. The active toxin binds to the midgut epithelial cells and creates pores, so the cells swell and lyse and the insect dies. Farmers therefore need fewer insecticide sprays.

**RNAi tobacco.** The nematode Meloidogyne incognita infects tobacco roots and reduces yield. RNA interference is a cellular defence in eukaryotes in which a complementary double-stranded RNA silences a specific mRNA. Using Agrobacterium vectors, nematode-specific genes were introduced into tobacco so that the plant produced both sense and antisense RNA. These formed dsRNA, which silenced the nematode’s mRNA, so the parasite could not survive in the transgenic roots.

questions.solution_md: Bt mechanism with cry genes; RNAi mechanism.

marking_scheme.step: Bt toxin source and cry genes
Protoxin, alkaline activation, pores and lysis
Sense and antisense RNA, dsRNA, silencing of nematode mRNA

questions.stem_md: Why did Eli Lilly produce the A and B chains of human insulin separately in E. coli instead of producing proinsulin?

options.text_md: The A chain is toxic to E. coli when produced alone.
Bacteria cannot remove the C peptide to turn proinsulin into mature insulin.
Proinsulin is identical to mature insulin.
E. coli cannot make disulphide-containing proteins in any form.

questions.solution_md: Proinsulin must lose its C peptide to mature; bacteria cannot do this, so the two final chains were made separately and joined — option (b).

questions.stem_md: Gene therapy for ADA deficiency using the patient’s own lymphocytes has to be repeated periodically. Why?

options.text_md: The ADA gene is destroyed by the retrovirus.
The genetically engineered lymphocytes are not immortal.
Lymphocytes reject the ADA enzyme.
The ADA gene is lost from all body cells after a month.

options.text_md: adenosine deaminase (ADA) deficiency
type 1 diabetes
emphysema
cystic fibrosis

questions.solution_md: It was given to a 4-year-old girl with ADA deficiency — option (a).

questions.stem_md: A health worker was accidentally exposed to HIV a few days ago. Her antibody test is negative because antibodies have not yet formed in large amounts. Which test would best detect an early infection?

A count of red blood cells
PCR to detect the virus’s genetic material

questions.stem_md: A radioactive probe complementary to a normal gene is added to clones of cells, and the result is checked by autoradiography. One clone does not show up on the film. What is the most likely explanation?

The probe destroyed the DNA of that clone.

questions.solution_md: A probe binds only to its complementary sequence; a mutated gene does not hybridise, so the clone is not seen — option (d).

ELISA, to amplify the gene
Bone marrow transplantation
Enzyme replacement therapy

questions.stem_md: What was the main drawback of insulin extracted from slaughtered cattle and pigs?

options.text_md: It caused allergy or other reactions in some patients.
It could not lower blood sugar at all.
It was made of a single chain without disulphide bridges.
It contained live bacteria.

options.text_md: Monthly injections of the ADA enzyme
A single infusion of engineered lymphocytes
Antibiotic treatment of the bone marrow
Introducing the ADA gene from marrow cells into cells at an early embryonic stage

questions.solution_md: Introducing the gene into early embryonic cells could make it permanent, unlike repeated enzyme injections or short-lived lymphocytes — option (d).

Fully specialised cells that can no longer divide
Cells found only in plant stems
Bacterial cells used to make recombinant proteins

Platelets that change into lymphocytes

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: False. The C peptide is present in proinsulin but is removed during maturation; the chains in mature insulin are joined by disulphide bridges.

questions.stem_md: About 30 recombinant therapeutics have been approved for human use worldwide; ______ of these are marketed in India.
questions.solution_md: Twelve.

**Reason (R):** ELISA works by amplifying small amounts of the pathogen’s DNA.

Choose the correct option.

Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

ELISA

questions.solution_md: Insulin $= 21 + 30 = 51$ amino acids (the C peptide is not part of mature insulin).

questions.stem_md: Describe how human insulin was produced by recombinant DNA technology, and why this insulin is preferred to insulin from animals.

answer.model_answer_md: Mature insulin has two chains, **A and B**, linked by **disulphide bridges**; it is made in the body as proinsulin with a **C peptide** that bacteria cannot remove. In **1983 Eli Lilly** prepared DNA sequences for **chains A and B**, put them into **plasmids of E. coli**, produced the two chains **separately**, extracted them and **joined them by disulphide bonds**. It is identical to human insulin, so it avoids the **allergic reactions** caused by animal insulin.

questions.stem_md: Describe the steps of gene therapy for ADA deficiency.

answer.model_answer_md: **Lymphocytes** are taken from the patient’s blood and **grown in culture** outside the body. A functional **ADA cDNA** is introduced into them using a **retroviral vector**. The engineered lymphocytes are **returned to the patient**, where they make ADA and help the immune system work. Because these cells are not immortal, the patient needs **periodic infusions** of engineered lymphocytes.

questions.solution_md: Culture, retroviral vector, return, repetition.

marking_scheme.step: ADA cDNA added by retroviral vector

questions.stem_md: Why can conventional methods not detect many infections early, and how does PCR overcome this?

questions.solution_md: Late detection; amplification by PCR.

questions.stem_md: A blood bank wants to screen donated blood for an infection. Explain how ELISA could be used, stating its principle and the two kinds of molecules it could look for.

answer.model_answer_md: ELISA is based on **antigen–antibody interaction**. questions.stem_md: A child is diagnosed with ADA deficiency. Explain the cause of the disorder, and compare the treatments available for it, judging which could give a permanent cure.

answer.model_answer_md:
**Cause.** Adenosine deaminase is an enzyme crucial for the immune system to function. The disorder is caused by deletion of the gene for ADA, so the child cannot make the enzyme and has a weak immune system.

**Treatments.** Bone marrow transplantation can help, but a suitable donor is not always available. Enzyme replacement therapy supplies functional ADA by injection, but it must be continued and is not completely curative. In gene therapy, lymphocytes from the patient’s blood are grown in culture, a functional ADA cDNA is introduced into them with a retroviral vector, and the cells are returned to the patient. This treats the cause rather than replacing the enzyme, but the engineered lymphocytes are not immortal, so periodic infusions are needed.

**Judgement.** None of these is permanent as usually given. A permanent cure could come only if the ADA gene isolated from marrow cells were introduced into cells at an early embryonic stage, so that all cells derived from them carry a working gene.

questions.stem_md: Explain how recombinant DNA technology, PCR and ELISA help in the early diagnosis of disease.

answer.model_answer_md:
**Need.** Early diagnosis allows effective treatment, but conventional methods such as serum and urine analysis cannot detect a disease until the pathogen has multiplied and symptoms have appeared.

**PCR.** The polymerase chain reaction amplifies very small amounts of a pathogen’s DNA or RNA to detectable levels. It is used to detect HIV in suspected AIDS patients and to detect mutations in genes of suspected cancer patients; it also helps identify many genetic disorders.

**Probes.** A single-stranded DNA or RNA tagged with a radioactive molecule is allowed to hybridise with its complementary DNA in a clone of cells and is detected by autoradiography. A clone with a mutated gene does not appear on the film, because the probe is not complementary to it.

**ELISA.** The enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay is based on antigen–antibody interaction. It can detect the antigens of a pathogen, or the antibodies made against it, in a sample.

**Patents.** Companies seek patents on products and technologies that use genetic materials, plants and other biological resources.
